passed.title: Use to_lowercase, to_uppercase and to_titlecase instead of the pandas names lower, upper and title
passed.trap: pandas habits such as `.str.lower()`, `.str.upper()`, `.str.title()` and `.str.startswith()` do not exist in Polars. They raise `AttributeError` as soon as the attribute is accessed. Use `Expr.str.to_lowercase`, `Expr.str.to_uppercase`, `Expr.str.to_titlecase`, `Expr.str.starts_with` and `Expr.str.ends_with`. A null input gives a null output in all of these; it is not coerced to `False`.

passed.title: count_matches treats the pattern as a regex unless literal=True
passed.trap: `Expr.str.count_matches` interprets `pattern` as a regular expression by default. Counting `"."` therefore counts every character, not the dots. Pass `literal=True` to count a plain substring. A null input gives null, not 0.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["a.b.c", "abc", None]})
print(
    df.with_columns(
        regex=pl.col("s").str.count_matches("."),
        literal=pl.col("s").str.count_matches(".", literal=True),
    )
)

passed.title: contains_any, replace_many and extract_many match literal strings, never regex
passed.trap: The Aho-Corasick methods `Expr.str.contains_any`, `Expr.str.replace_many`, `Expr.str.extract_many` and `Expr.str.find_many` only match string literals. A pattern like `r"\d"` searches for a backslash followed by `d`, not for a digit. These calls raise no error, so the result is silently wrong. Use `Expr.str.contains`, `Expr.str.extract_all` or `Expr.str.replace_all` when you need regex semantics.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["a1", "b\\d"]})
print(
    df.with_columns(
        any_literal=pl.col("s").str.contains_any([r"\d"]),
        regex=pl.col("s").str.contains(r"\d"),
    )
)

passed.title: find_many returns byte offsets, not character positions
passed.trap: `Expr.str.find_many` returns a `List<UInt32>` of byte offsets for each match start. With non-ASCII text these offsets are larger than the character index. Do not feed them into character-based slicing such as `Expr.str.slice` and expect the right substring. Compare `Expr.str.len_bytes` with `Expr.str.len_chars` to see the difference.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["cafe bar", "café bar"]})
print(
    df.with_columns(
        offset=pl.col("s").str.find_many(["bar"]),
        n_bytes=pl.col("s").str.len_bytes(),
        n_chars=pl.col("s").str.len_chars(),
    )
)

passed.title: json_decode requires an explicit dtype in 1.38
passed.trap: Since 1.33.0 the `dtype` argument of `Expr.str.json_decode` is mandatory. Older code that calls `.str.json_decode()` and relies on schema inference fails with `TypeError`. The `infer_schema_length` argument is deprecated and ignored. Pass the target type, for example a `pl.Struct` of `pl.Field`s. Invalid JSON raises an error.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": ['{"a":1,"b":true}', '{"a":2,"b":false}']})
try:
    df.select(pl.col("j").str.json_decode())
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
dtype = pl.Struct([pl.Field("a", pl.Int64), pl.Field("b", pl.Boolean)])
print(df.select(pl.col("j").str.json_decode(dtype)).unnest("j"))

passed.title: json_path_match always returns String, even for numbers and booleans
passed.trap: `Expr.str.json_path_match` casts every extracted value to `String`, whatever its JSON type. Doing arithmetic or numeric comparisons on the result is wrong: comparisons are lexical, and math fails. Cast explicitly with `Expr.cast`. If you need typed fields, use `Expr.str.json_decode` with a dtype. A missing path or a null input gives null.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": ['{"a":10}', '{"a":9}', None]})
m = df.select(a=pl.col("j").str.json_path_match("$.a"))
print(m.schema)
print(m.select(pl.col("a").max()))
print(m.select(pl.col("a").cast(pl.Int64).max()))

passed.title: extract_groups names unnamed groups "1", "2", ... as strings
passed.trap: `Expr.str.extract_groups` returns a `Struct` whose fields are all `String`. Unnamed capture groups get their position as a string name (`"1"`, `"2"`). Access them with `Expr.struct.field("1")` or use named groups such as `(?<key>...)`. Rows where the pattern does not match give null fields, and `Expr.str.extract` likewise returns null rather than an empty string.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["k=1", "no match"]})
out = df.select(g=pl.col("s").str.extract_groups(r"(\w)=(\d)"))
print(out.unnest("g").columns)
print(out.select(pl.col("g").struct.field("2")))
named = df.select(g=pl.col("s").str.extract_groups(r"(?<key>\w)=(?<val>\d)"))
print(named.unnest("g"))

passed.title: Replace deprecated str.explode with str.split("").explode(), noting that empty strings become null
passed.trap: `Expr.str.explode` is deprecated since 0.20.31. The replacement is `Expr.str.split` with `""` followed by `Expr.explode`. The behaviour differs: an empty string now yields a null row instead of being preserved. If you need the old behaviour, handle empty lists with `pl.when` before exploding.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": ["ab", ""]})
out = df.select(pl.col("a").str.split("").explode())
print(out)
print(out.null_count())

passed.title: decode raises on invalid input unless strict=False
passed.trap: `Expr.str.decode` defaults to `strict=True`, so one malformed hex or base64 value fails the whole query. Pass `strict=False` to turn undecodable values into null. The result dtype is `Binary`, not `String`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"h": ["ff00", "zz"]})
try:
    df.select(pl.col("h").str.decode("hex"))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
print(df.select(pl.col("h").str.decode("hex", strict=False)))
